posts.title: Canada Express Entry explained: CRS points, draws and what to expect
posts.excerpt: Express Entry is Canada's main route to permanent residence for skilled workers. Here's how profiles, CRS scores and draws work, in plain English.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Express Entry is an online system Canada uses to manage applications for permanent residence from skilled workers. You create a profile, get a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score, and wait in a pool. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) holds regular draws and invites the highest-scoring or targeted candidates to apply.

The three main programmes

Express Entry covers:

  • Federal Skilled Worker Program, for skilled workers with foreign experience
  • Canadian Experience Class, for people with skilled work experience in Canada
  • Federal Skilled Trades Program, for qualified tradespeople

Provincial Nominee Programs can also use Express Entry. A provincial nomination adds a large number of points.

How the CRS score works

Your CRS score is based on factors like:

  • Age
  • Education
  • Language ability in English and/or French
  • Work experience, especially in Canada
  • Your spouse's education, language and experience, if applicable
  • Extras like a provincial nomination, French skills or a sibling in Canada

Language test results often make the biggest difference you can control. Many Nigerian applicants improve their score significantly by retaking IELTS or CELPIP to reach higher bands, or by learning French.

Draws: general and category-based

IRCC holds draws throughout the year. Some invite the top candidates overall, others target specific groups, such as Canadian Experience Class, French speakers or particular occupations like healthcare. Cut-off scores change from draw to draw, so look at recent results rather than old ones.

After you're invited

An Invitation to Apply gives you a limited time to submit a full application with documents such as:

  • Educational Credential Assessment (ECA)
  • Police certificates from countries where you've lived
  • Medical exam results
  • Proof of funds, unless you're exempt
  • Reference letters for your work experience

Missing or inconsistent documents are a common cause of refusal.

Proof of funds

If you're applying under the Federal Skilled Worker or Skilled Trades programmes without a valid Canadian job offer, you must show settlement funds. The amounts are updated each year, so check IRCC's current table.

Beware of fake consultants

Only licensed consultants (members of the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants) or lawyers can charge you for immigration advice. No one can guarantee an invitation.

The bottom line

Maximise what you can control, especially language scores, keep your documents ready and follow official IRCC updates on draws.

This is general information, not immigration advice.

  • IRCC — CRS tool

posts.title: Watching AFCON from the UK: how diaspora fans make match days special
posts.excerpt: When the Super Eagles play at the Africa Cup of Nations, diaspora communities light up. Here's how fans in the UK watch, celebrate and support the team.
posts.content:
Quick gist: The Africa Cup of Nations brings Nigerian communities abroad together like few other events. Fans gather in homes, restaurants, community halls and pubs to watch the Super Eagles, often in full green and white. Planning ahead for kick-off times, venues and childcare makes match days easier.

Finding where to watch

  • Community halls and churches: some host big-screen viewings for major matches.
  • African restaurants and lounges: often show matches and serve food.
  • Friends' homes: the classic option, with jollof and suya.

Kick-off times

Most AFCON matches are played in Africa, so kick-off times are usually close to UK time, give or take an hour or two. That's easier than World Cups in faraway time zones.

Match day traditions

  • Green and white jerseys, flags and face paint
  • Shared food: jollof, pepper soup, suya, small chops
  • Loud debates about the coach's team selection
  • Victory celebrations and, sometimes, heartbreak

Bring the kids

AFCON is a great chance for children raised abroad to connect with Nigeria. Explain the history, the players and why it matters to the family.

Respect and safety

Keep celebrations friendly, respect rival fans and be mindful of neighbours when celebrating late.

Following the tournament

Check CAF's official channels for fixtures, results and broadcasting information.

The bottom line

Whether it's a living room or a packed hall, watching AFCON with fellow Nigerians abroad is one of the best feelings of home.

posts.title: Accountants moving to the UK: ICAN, ACCA and recognition explained
posts.excerpt: Qualified accountant in Nigeria? Here's how your ICAN qualification compares, what UK employers look for and how ACCA or other bodies fit in.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Many Nigerian accountants hold ICAN (Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria) or ACCA qualifications. ACCA is well known to UK employers. ICAN members may be able to gain exemptions or recognition with UK bodies depending on current agreements. UK experience, software skills and an understanding of UK tax and standards are important for landing roles.

What UK employers look for

  • A recognised professional qualification (ACCA, ICAEW, CIMA or equivalent)
  • Experience with UK or international accounting standards
  • Software skills (Excel, accounting packages, ERP systems)
  • Knowledge of UK tax, payroll or audit, depending on the role

ACCA

ACCA is a global qualification widely recognised in the UK. If you're already ACCA-qualified, you can apply for UK roles directly. If you're part-qualified, you can continue your studies in the UK.

ICAN

ICAN is Nigeria's main chartered accountancy body. Recognition and exemptions with UK bodies change over time, so check with ACCA, ICAEW or CIMA about what credit you can get for your ICAN qualification.

Getting UK experience

  • Consider interim, contract or temporary roles to build UK experience.
  • Volunteer as a treasurer for a charity or community group.
  • Learn UK-specific areas like VAT, payroll and Making Tax Digital.

Visas

Many finance roles are eligible for sponsorship on the Skilled Worker visa if the salary and occupation requirements are met.

Networking

Join professional networks, including Nigerian accountants' associations in the UK, and connect with recruiters who specialise in finance.

The bottom line

Your Nigerian qualification and experience are valuable. Check recognition with UK bodies, build UK-specific skills and target roles that value international experience.

posts.title: Nigerian diaspora voting: can Nigerians abroad vote, and what's the debate?
posts.excerpt: Millions of Nigerians live abroad, but they can't currently vote from outside Nigeria. Here's where the diaspora voting debate stands and why it keeps coming up.
posts.content:
Quick gist: At the time of writing, Nigerians living abroad cannot vote in Nigerian elections from overseas. To vote, you must be registered and physically present at your polling unit in Nigeria. Bills to allow diaspora voting have been proposed many times but would need changes to Nigeria's laws and, according to many legal experts, the constitution.

How voting works now

Nigeria's electoral law requires voters to register with the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and vote in person at the polling unit where they're registered. There's no postal vote and no voting at embassies. So a Nigerian living in London who wants to vote has to travel home for election day.

Why diaspora voting keeps coming up

Nigerians abroad send billions of dollars home every year, support families and invest in property and businesses. Many argue that people who contribute so much should have a say in who governs. Diaspora groups have campaigned on this for years.

What would need to change

Supporters of diaspora voting say Nigeria would need to:

  • Amend the electoral law to allow voting outside Nigeria
  • Possibly amend the constitution
  • Set up systems for registration abroad, such as at embassies and consulates
  • Decide how to handle security, logistics and cost across many countries

Several bills have been introduced in the National Assembly over the years, but none has completed the full process into law at the time of writing.

The arguments against, or for caution

Critics and cautious voices raise concerns about:

  • The cost of running elections in many countries
  • The risk of fraud or disputes over results
  • The capacity of embassies to handle registration and voting
  • Whether to prioritise improving elections at home first

How other African countries do it

Several African countries allow some form of diaspora voting, often at embassies. Supporters point to these examples; critics point to low turnout and high costs in some of them.

What you can do now

  • Follow NiDCOM and diaspora organisations that campaign on the issue
  • Engage with your representatives in Nigeria
  • If you'll be home during an election, check INEC's rules on registration and transferring your voter registration

The bottom line

For now, voting means being in Nigeria on election day. Diaspora voting remains a live debate, and any change would need new laws and a lot of preparation.

This reflects the position at the time of writing. Check INEC for the latest information.

posts.title: Nigeria's national anthem change: why "Nigeria, We Hail Thee" is back
posts.excerpt: In 2024 Nigeria brought back its independence-era anthem, "Nigeria, We Hail Thee." Here's the history and why the change sparked debate.
posts.content:
Quick gist: In May 2024, President Bola Tinubu signed a law restoring "Nigeria, We Hail Thee" as Nigeria's national anthem. It was the anthem adopted at independence in 1960 and had been replaced in 1978 by "Arise, O Compatriots." Supporters see it as reconnecting with history; critics questioned the timing and the anthem's colonial-era origins.

A tale of two anthems

  • "Nigeria, We Hail Thee" (1960–1978): the independence anthem. Its words were written by Lillian Jean Williams, a British expatriate, and its music by Frances Berda.
  • "Arise, O Compatriots" (1978–2024): adopted under the military government, with words drawn from entries by Nigerians and music arranged by the Nigerian Police Band.

The 2024 change

The National Assembly passed a bill restoring the old anthem, and the President signed it into law in May 2024. It was first sung officially at events marking Democracy Day.

Why supporters backed it

  • It reflects Nigeria's independence and early national identity.
  • Some argued its lyrics emphasise unity across diversity.

Why critics objected

  • The process was quick, with limited public consultation.
  • Some felt there were more urgent priorities given economic hardship.
  • Others noted the lyrics were written by a non-Nigerian.

Teaching children abroad

Many diaspora parents who grew up singing "Arise, O Compatriots" now teach their children the new (old) anthem. It's a good conversation starter about Nigeria's history.

The pledge

The National Pledge, recited in schools, remains in use.

The bottom line

The anthem change sparked debate at home and abroad. Whatever your view, it's a reminder that national symbols carry history and meaning.

posts.title: How to write a UK-style CV: what recruiters expect
posts.excerpt: A Nigerian CV and a UK CV are not the same. No photo, no date of birth, two pages and achievements over duties. Here's how to adapt yours.
posts.content:
Quick gist: UK recruiters expect a clean, two-page CV with no photo, no date of birth, no marital status and no religion. Lead with a short profile, list experience in reverse order, and focus on achievements with numbers rather than long lists of duties. Tailor it for every job.

What to leave out

These are common on Nigerian CVs but not expected in the UK, and some can even work against you:

  • Photo
  • Date of birth and age
  • Marital status, number of children, religion, state of origin
  • Full home address (your town is enough)
  • "References available on request", which is assumed

UK equality law aims to stop discrimination based on things like age and religion, so recruiters prefer CVs without them.

The structure that works

  1. Name and contact details: phone, email, town, LinkedIn.
  2. Personal profile: three or four lines on who you are, your key skills and what you're looking for.
  3. Work experience: most recent first, with job title, employer, location and dates.
  4. Education and qualifications: most recent first. Add the UK equivalent if helpful.
  5. Skills: software, languages, certifications.

Keep it to two pages for most roles.

Achievements, not duties

Compare these:

  • Duties: "Responsible for managing customer accounts."
  • Achievement: "Managed 120 customer accounts and grew renewals by 18% in one year."

Numbers make your impact clear. Think about money saved, targets beaten, people trained and processes improved.

Explaining Nigerian experience

UK employers may not know your former employer. Add a short line such as "one of Nigeria's largest telecoms providers" or "a 200-bed teaching hospital". Mention international standards or clients if relevant.

Tailor for every application

Read the job description and match its keywords. Many employers use software that scans CVs for relevant terms. If the advert says "stakeholder management", use that phrase, as long as it's true.

Right to work

You don't need to put your visa details on your CV, but you can add a line such as "Full right to work in the UK" or "Require sponsorship". Being clear saves time for both sides.

Cover letters and applications

Many UK jobs, especially in the NHS and public sector, use application forms with a "supporting statement". Treat it seriously: use the person specification as a checklist and give examples for each point.

Final checks

  • Use UK spelling (organise, programme, CV)
  • Save as PDF unless asked otherwise
  • Use a professional email address
  • Ask a friend in the UK to read it

The bottom line

A clear, tailored, achievement-focused CV gets interviews. Strip out what UK recruiters don't need and show what you've delivered.

posts.title: D'Tigress: how Nigeria's women became Africa's basketball queens
posts.excerpt: Nigeria's women's basketball team has dominated African basketball for years and made history at the Olympics. Here's the story of D'Tigress.
posts.content:
Quick gist: D'Tigress, Nigeria's senior women's basketball team, have won the Women's AfroBasket championship several times in a row since 2017, cementing their place as Africa's top side. At the Paris 2024 Olympics they reached the quarter-finals, the best Olympic result by any African basketball team, men or women.

A team built across continents

Like many Nigerian national teams, D'Tigress bring together players from home and from the diaspora. Some grew up in Nigeria, others in the US, the UK or elsewhere, and many play professionally in the US, Europe or Australia. That mix of experience has helped the team compete with the world's best.

Dominating Africa

The run began at AfroBasket 2017, and D'Tigress kept winning title after title in the tournaments that followed. They play with intensity, strong defence and depth, and they've become the team every African rival measures itself against.

World Cup and Olympic progress

At the 2018 FIBA Women's World Cup, Nigeria reached the quarter-finals, a big moment for African basketball. They also qualified for the Olympics in Tokyo and Paris. In Paris 2024, D'Tigress won group games against strong opponents and reached the quarter-finals, writing a new chapter in African basketball history.

Off-court battles

The team's success has also shone a light on problems behind the scenes, including disputes over pay, allowances and organisation. Players and fans have called for better support for women's sport in Nigeria, and those conversations continue.

Why the diaspora should follow D'Tigress

  • Many players have roots in diaspora communities and are role models for young Nigerian girls abroad
  • Women's sport is growing fast in the UK, US and Canada, and D'Tigress games are increasingly easy to stream
  • Supporting them helps push for better funding and recognition at home

How to follow them

Follow FIBA's channels for fixtures and streaming information, and the team's official social media for squad news.

The bottom line

D'Tigress are one of Nigeria's most successful national teams of the last decade. If you haven't been following them, now is a great time to start.

posts.title: Council tax in the UK: what it is and how to pay less legally
posts.excerpt: Council tax often surprises new arrivals. Here's what it pays for, how much you might pay and the discounts and exemptions you could be eligible for.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Council tax is a yearly charge from your local council for services like bin collection, street lighting and local policing. The amount depends on your home's valuation band and your council. Students, people living alone and some others can get discounts or exemptions, so always check before paying the full amount.

Who pays

Usually the adults living in a property pay council tax, not the landlord. In shared houses rented by the room, the landlord may be responsible instead, so check your tenancy agreement.

How much it costs

Every home in England and Scotland is in a council tax band based on its value at a fixed past date (Wales has its own bands). Your council sets the rate for each band each year. You can check your home's band on GOV.UK.

Bills usually arrive in spring for the year from April, and you can normally pay in 10 monthly instalments, or ask for 12.

Discounts that can save you money

  • Single person discount: if you're the only adult in the home, you get 25% off.
  • Full-time students: a home occupied only by full-time students is usually exempt. If you live with one non-student, the bill may be reduced. Get a council tax exemption certificate from your university.
  • Student spouses and dependants: in some cases, the non-UK spouse or dependant of a student may also be disregarded. Check with your council.
  • Council Tax Reduction: a support scheme for people on low incomes. Eligibility for people subject to "no recourse to public funds" conditions is limited, so check carefully before applying.

Paying the right amount

  • Tell the council when you move in and move out
  • Check the band is correct. If you think it's wrong, you can challenge it
  • Set up a direct debit so you never miss a payment

What happens if you don't pay

Missing payments can lead to reminders, then the council demanding the whole year's bill at once, then court action and extra costs. If you're struggling, contact the council early; they may agree a payment plan.

Council tax and visas

Unpaid debts and court judgments can cause problems later, including with credit applications. Keeping your council tax up to date is part of building a clean financial record in the UK.

The bottom line

Find your band, check every discount you might qualify for and set up a direct debit. It's one of the biggest household bills after rent.

This is general information. Rules differ between England, Scotland and Wales.

posts.title: Raising children with two cultures: tips from Nigerian parents abroad
posts.excerpt: Your children may sound British or Canadian, but you want them to feel Nigerian too. Practical ideas from parents who are making it work.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Children raised abroad often grow up with two identities, and that's a strength, not a problem. Parents who succeed usually make culture part of everyday life (food, language, music, stories and visits home) while also listening to their children's experiences of growing up in a different country.

Accept that your children's childhood is different

Your children won't grow up the way you did, and that's okay. They'll have school friends from many backgrounds, different slang and different pressures. Trying to recreate your exact childhood often leads to frustration on both sides. Aim for connection, not copying.

Speak your language at home

Language is often the first thing to fade. Many parents find these help:

  • One parent speaks Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa or another language most of the time
  • Pidgin or Nigerian English for everyday jokes and sayings
  • Video calls with grandparents in the language
  • Children's books, songs and cartoons in Nigerian languages

Even if your children answer in English, they're still learning.

Make food a family project

Cooking jollof, egusi or puff-puff together teaches more than recipes. It creates stories, smells and memories that children carry for life.

Tell the stories

Share stories about your childhood, your village or town, your family history and Nigeria's history. Children love hearing what you got up to at their age.

Visit home when you can

Trips to Nigeria, even short ones, help children connect the stories to real places and people. If travel isn't possible, video calls, photos and family WhatsApp groups help keep relationships alive.

Find your community

Churches, mosques, cultural associations and Saturday schools often run language classes, cultural days and youth groups. Being around other Nigerian children helps your children feel that their heritage is normal and shared.

Talk about identity and racism

Children of African heritage may face racism or questions about where they're "really from". Talk openly at home, help them find words for their experience, and work with schools if problems arise. Celebrate Black History Month and Nigerian Independence Day together.

Balance discipline and understanding

Parenting styles that were normal back home may be seen differently abroad. In the UK, for example, physical punishment of children is restricted by law, and schools take safeguarding seriously. Many parents find positive discipline, clear rules and consistent consequences work well.

The bottom line

Children can be proudly Nigerian and comfortably British, Canadian or American at the same time. Make culture part of daily life, listen as much as you teach and enjoy watching them build their own identity.

posts.title: Highlife: the sound that came before Afrobeats
posts.excerpt: Before Afrobeats and before Afrobeat, there was highlife. Here's the story of the guitar-and-horns sound that soundtracked West Africa's independence era.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Highlife is a West African music style that grew up in Ghana in the early 20th century and spread to Nigeria. It blends local rhythms and melodies with Western instruments like guitars and horns. It was the soundtrack of the independence era, and it shaped Afrobeat, Afrobeats and much of today's African pop.

Where it started

Highlife began in what is now Ghana, where musicians combined traditional rhythms with church hymns, sea shanties and brass band music. The name is said to come from the "high life" of the elite clubs where dance bands played.

Highlife in Nigeria

In Nigeria, highlife became the party sound of the 1950s and 1960s. Big band leaders such as Bobby Benson, Victor Olaiya and later Rex Lawson, Victor Uwaifo and Oliver De Coque became stars. Eastern Nigeria developed a strong guitar-highlife tradition, with fast, intricate guitar lines that are still loved today.

Independence and celebration

As Ghana and Nigeria moved towards independence, highlife was everywhere: at weddings, parties and political rallies. It carried messages of pride, love, hardship and celebration.

Fela's roots

Fela Kuti played highlife early in his career before creating Afrobeat. You can hear highlife's DNA in his work, and later in Afrobeats.

Highlife today

Highlife never went away. It's still the sound of many weddings and owambes, and modern artists often borrow its guitar lines and melodies. Some contemporary stars mix highlife with Afrobeats, hip-hop and R&B, introducing it to a new generation.

Where to start listening

Search streaming services for highlife classics and "best of Nigerian highlife" playlists. Ask your parents and aunties: they'll have strong opinions.

The bottom line

If you love Afrobeats, you already love highlife, even if you didn't know it. It's the foundation much of modern West African pop is built on.

posts.title: UK Graduate visa: who qualifies and how to make the most of it
posts.excerpt: The Graduate visa lets international students stay and work in the UK after their course. Here's who qualifies, how to apply and how to use the time well.
posts.content:
Quick gist: The UK Graduate visa lets eligible international students stay and work, or look for work, after completing a degree in the UK. You must apply from inside the UK before your Student visa expires, and your university must have reported that you completed your course. It doesn't require a job offer or sponsor, but it can't be extended.

Who qualifies

Generally, you need to:

  • Be in the UK on a Student visa
  • Have successfully completed an eligible UK course (usually a bachelor's, master's or PhD)
  • Have studied in the UK for the required period
  • Have your university confirm your completion to the Home Office

Check GOV.UK for the current rules, as the length of the visa and other details have been changing.

What you can do on it

  • Work in almost any job, at any skill level
  • Look for work
  • Be self-employed
  • Do voluntary work

You can't usually work as a professional sportsperson, and you can't access most public funds.

How long it lasts

The length depends on your qualification and the rules in force when you apply. PhD graduates have historically been given longer than bachelor's and master's graduates. Recent policy changes have shortened the standard period, so check the latest guidance.

How to apply

Apply online from inside the UK, before your Student visa expires. You'll pay the application fee and the Immigration Health Surcharge. You'll prove your identity through the app or an appointment, and once approved you'll get an eVisa.

Using the time well

The Graduate visa can't be extended, so plan from day one:

  • Aim for a sponsored role. If you want to stay long-term, target employers who hold a sponsor licence and roles that qualify for the Skilled Worker visa.
  • Check salary thresholds. "New entrant" rules may allow a lower salary threshold for recent graduates switching from the Graduate visa.
  • Build UK experience. Even a non-sponsored job builds your CV and references.
  • Network. Careers services, alumni groups and professional bodies are valuable.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting until your Student visa has nearly expired
  • Applying before the university has reported your completion
  • Assuming any job will lead to sponsorship

The bottom line

The Graduate visa is a valuable window, but it's limited. Plan your next step early and target sponsors from the start.

This is general information, not immigration advice.

posts.title: Getting your UK driving licence: swapping or passing the test
posts.excerpt: Can you drive in the UK on your Nigerian licence? For how long? And how do you get a full UK licence? Here's what new arrivals need to know.
posts.content:
Quick gist: If you're a resident in Great Britain with a valid Nigerian licence, you can usually drive small vehicles for up to 12 months from when you became resident. Nigeria isn't on the list of countries whose licences can be exchanged directly, so to keep driving after that, you'll need a UK provisional licence and to pass the theory and practical tests.

The 12-month rule

GOV.UK sets out how long you can drive on a licence from a non-EU country. For most residents with a full, valid licence, it's 12 months from the date you became resident. After that, you need a UK licence. Check GOV.UK for your exact situation.

Why you can't just swap

The UK allows direct exchange of licences only from certain "designated countries". Nigeria isn't one of them at the time of writing, so Nigerian licence holders need to pass UK tests.

Step 1: provisional licence

Apply online for a provisional licence through GOV.UK. You'll need your identity documents and to have been resident in Great Britain for the required time. It's cheaper online than by post.

Step 2: theory test

The theory test has two parts: multiple-choice questions on the Highway Code and a hazard perception test using video clips. Practice apps and the official Highway Code book help a lot. Book only through the official GOV.UK service; unofficial sites charge extra.

Step 3: lessons

Even experienced drivers from Nigeria often need lessons to learn UK test standards: mirror checks, roundabouts, lane discipline and speed limits. A few lessons with an approved driving instructor can save you failed tests.

Step 4: practical test

Test slots can be hard to get in busy areas. Check regularly for cancellations on the official booking service. You'll drive for about 40 minutes, including independent driving and manoeuvres.

Insurance

UK car insurance can be expensive for new arrivals with no UK driving history. Ask insurers if they'll consider your Nigerian driving record, compare quotes and consider a black box policy.

Avoid these mistakes

  • Driving on a Nigerian licence after your 12 months are up
  • Driving without insurance, which carries heavy penalties
  • Using unofficial test booking sites

The bottom line

Use your 12 months wisely: get your provisional licence, pass the theory test and start lessons early so you're not stuck when your time runs out.

This is general information. Check GOV.UK for current rules.

posts.title: Interview tips for UK jobs: the STAR method and other things that work
posts.excerpt: UK interviews often focus on examples, not just qualifications. Here's how to use the STAR method, prepare for common questions and stand out.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Many UK employers use competency-based interviews, asking you to describe real situations where you showed a skill. The STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) helps you answer clearly. Prepare five or six strong stories, research the organisation and ask good questions at the end.

Competency-based questions

You'll often hear questions like:

  • "Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer."
  • "Give an example of when you worked under pressure."
  • "Describe a time you disagreed with a colleague."

The interviewer wants evidence from your experience, not a general statement like "I work well under pressure".

The STAR method

  • Situation: set the scene briefly. Where were you, what was happening?
  • Task: what was your responsibility?
  • Action: what did you do? Use "I", not "we". This is the most important part.
  • Result: what happened? Use numbers if you can, and what you learned.

Keep each answer to about two minutes.

Use your Nigerian experience confidently

Experience from Nigeria is real experience. Explain the context briefly (size of organisation, number of customers or patients) and focus on what you achieved. Many interviewers value people who've worked in challenging environments.

Research the organisation

Read the job description, the person specification and the employer's website. For the NHS and public sector, learn their values; interviewers often ask how you show them.

Common questions to prepare

  • "Tell us about yourself": a two-minute summary of your career and why this role
  • "Why do you want to work here?"
  • "What are your strengths and weaknesses?"
  • "Where do you see yourself in five years?"

Ask good questions

At the end, ask one or two thoughtful questions, such as about training, team structure or what success looks like in the first six months. Avoid asking about salary in the first interview unless they raise it.

Online interviews

Many first-round interviews are on video. Test your camera and internet, sit somewhere quiet with a plain background and look at the camera when speaking.

After the interview

Send a short thank-you email. If you're not successful, politely ask for feedback; it helps you improve for the next one.

The bottom line

Prepare stories, practise STAR answers out loud and walk in confident about the experience you bring.

posts.title: Japa and family back home: setting boundaries without guilt
posts.excerpt: Once you move abroad, the requests start. School fees, hospital bills, "small" loans. Here's how to support family without sinking yourself.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Supporting family back home is a big part of life for many Nigerians abroad. But living costs abroad are high, and many people quietly struggle to keep up with requests. A clear budget, honest conversations and fair, consistent boundaries can help you keep giving without damaging your own finances or wellbeing.

The pressure is real

Back home, many people assume life abroad means easy money. They don't see the rent, council tax, energy bills, childcare costs and visa fees. The result is a constant stream of requests, and guilt when you say no.

Start with your own numbers

Before you can help others, you need to know what you can afford. Write down your monthly income and essential costs: rent, bills, food, transport, savings and debt repayments. Whatever is left is what's realistically available for support.

Decide what you'll give, in advance

Many people find it easier to set a monthly amount for family support rather than reacting to every request. For example:

  • A fixed monthly amount for parents
  • A yearly amount for school fees
  • A small emergency fund for genuine crises

When the money for the month is used, you can honestly say so.

Have the honest conversation

It can help to explain your real costs to close family. You don't have to share every detail, but describing rent, bills and visa fees in naira helps people understand.

Pay directly when you can

For school fees, hospital bills or rent, paying the institution directly can make sure the money is used as intended.

Help people stand on their own feet

Sometimes the best support is helping someone earn: paying for a course, a trade tool or start-up stock for a small business. It can reduce future requests and build dignity.

Watch out for scams

Some "emergencies" are scams, especially messages from new numbers claiming to be relatives. Call the person directly before sending money.

Look after yourself

Constant pressure can affect your mental health and relationships. Talk to your partner, friends or a counsellor. Your wellbeing matters too.

The bottom line

Giving is a beautiful part of our culture, but it should be planned, not panicked. Set your budget, set your boundaries and give with a clear conscience.

posts.title: What is NiDCOM? The Nigerians in Diaspora Commission explained
posts.excerpt: NiDCOM is the Nigerian government agency that deals with Nigerians abroad. Here's what it does, when it can help and how to contact it.
posts.content:
Quick gist: The Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NiDCOM) is a federal agency set up to engage Nigerians living abroad, protect their interests and encourage them to contribute to Nigeria's development. It works alongside Nigeria's embassies and high commissions, which remain your first stop for consular services like passports.

Why NiDCOM was created

Nigeria has one of the largest diasporas in Africa. Nigerians abroad send home billions of dollars every year and many want to invest, volunteer or return. The commission was established by law in 2017 and started work afterwards, giving the diaspora a dedicated voice in government.

What it does

NiDCOM's work includes:

  • Engaging diaspora communities and organisations
  • Advocating for Nigerians abroad who face crises, such as during conflicts or mass deportations
  • Supporting evacuations and the return of distressed Nigerians, working with other agencies
  • Promoting diaspora investment, skills transfer and knowledge sharing
  • Organising events such as Diaspora Day

What it doesn't do

NiDCOM isn't where you renew your passport or get consular documents. For those, go to the Nigerian embassy or high commission in your country, or the Nigeria Immigration Service portal.

When NiDCOM might help

  • If you're caught up in a crisis abroad affecting many Nigerians
  • If you want to connect with diaspora investment or volunteering schemes
  • If your diaspora organisation wants to engage with government

How to contact it

NiDCOM's official website and social media accounts list contact details and announcements. Be careful of fake pages claiming to represent the commission.

The bigger picture

The diaspora's relationship with government back home is complicated. Many Nigerians abroad want better consular services, diaspora voting and easier investment rules. Agencies like NiDCOM are part of that conversation.

The bottom line

NiDCOM is the government's dedicated diaspora agency. For everyday consular needs, go to your embassy; for diaspora engagement and crisis advocacy, NiDCOM is the place to look.

Check NiDCOM's official website for the latest information.

posts.title: Buying land in Nigeria from abroad: documents to check before you pay
posts.excerpt: Land scams are one of the biggest risks for Nigerians abroad. Here's what documents to ask for, the checks to make and how to protect your money.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Before you pay for land in Nigeria, verify who really owns it, what title documents exist and whether the land is free from government acquisition or disputes. Use an independent lawyer and surveyor you choose yourself, search the land registry, and never rely only on a relative or agent's word.

Why diaspora buyers are targets

Fraudsters know Nigerians abroad can't easily visit the site. Common scams include selling the same plot to several buyers, selling land under government acquisition, and fake documents. Even honest family members can be misled.

Key documents to understand

  • Certificate of Occupancy (C of O): issued by a state government, showing a right of occupancy over the land.
  • Governor's Consent: needed when land with a C of O changes hands. Buying without it leaves your title weak.
  • Deed of Assignment: the agreement transferring the seller's interest to you. It should be properly stamped and registered.
  • Survey plan: shows the exact location and boundaries, prepared by a registered surveyor.
  • Excision or Gazette: in some states, community land must be excised from government acquisition before it can be sold.

Requirements differ by state, so your lawyer should explain what applies to your plot.

Checks to make

  1. Land registry search. Your lawyer can search the state land registry to confirm the title and whether it's encumbered.
  2. Survey verification. Have the survey plan checked at the Surveyor-General's office to confirm the land isn't under acquisition.
  3. Physical inspection. Someone you trust, ideally independent, should visit, take dated photos and talk to neighbours.
  4. Family land. If buying from a family, make sure the right family representatives sign and that there's a family resolution.

Paying safely

  • Pay into a traceable account in the seller's or company's name, never cash
  • Get receipts and the signed agreement
  • Pay in stages tied to documents where possible

Estates and developers

Buying in an estate can be easier, but check the developer's title, track record and whether infrastructure promises are realistic. Read the contract carefully.

After you buy

Register your deed, keep copies of everything safely (including scans abroad) and visit or have someone check the land regularly. Fencing and building help show possession.

The bottom line

Land can be a great investment, but only if your title is solid. Spend on proper legal and survey checks; they cost far less than losing your money.

This is general information, not legal advice. Speak to a qualified lawyer in Nigeria.

posts.title: Tobi Amusan and Nigeria's track stars: a guide for new fans
posts.excerpt: From Tobi Amusan's world record to Nigeria's sprinting history, here's a quick guide to Nigerian athletics for fans in the diaspora.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Nigeria has a proud athletics history, from Olympic relay medals to individual world champions. In 2022, Tobi Amusan won the 100m hurdles world title and set a world record, one of the biggest moments in Nigerian sport in recent years. Many of Nigeria's best athletes train and compete in the US and Europe, and diaspora fans can follow them at major meets all year.

Tobi Amusan's historic year

At the 2022 World Championships in Eugene, Oregon, Tobi Amusan ran 12.12 seconds in the 100m hurdles semi-final, breaking the world record, and then won the final. She became Nigeria's first individual world champion in athletics. She had already won Commonwealth and African titles, and she remains one of the stars of the event.

A sprinting nation

Nigeria has produced many world-class sprinters and relay teams. Older fans remember Olympic relay medals and the sprinters who made Nigeria a force on the track. Today, a new generation competes in the US college system and on the professional Diamond League circuit.

Field events too

Nigeria has strong athletes in field events as well. Long jumpers and other field athletes have won medals at the Commonwealth Games and on the global stage.

The US college connection

Many Nigerian athletes earn scholarships to American universities, where they train in top facilities and compete in NCAA championships. It's a path that has developed many champions.

Where to watch

  • World Championships and the Olympics: the biggest stages
  • Commonwealth Games: where Nigerian athletes often win medals, and UK-based fans can sometimes watch in person
  • Diamond League: a series of elite meets across the world, including in the UK
  • African Championships: for the continental titles

Check World Athletics for schedules.

Challenges at home

Nigerian athletes have sometimes spoken out about funding, kit and administrative problems. Fans continue to push for better support so talent isn't lost.

The bottom line

Nigerian athletics is full of talent and stories. Follow the major meets, cheer loudly and keep an eye on the next generation.

posts.title: ISAs, pensions and savings: a starter guide for Nigerians in the UK
posts.excerpt: Once the bills are paid, where should your savings go? A simple guide to emergency funds, ISAs and workplace pensions for new arrivals in the UK.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Start with an emergency fund of a few months' essential costs in an easy-access savings account. Then make the most of tax-free ISAs and your workplace pension, which comes with free money from your employer. Avoid get-rich-quick schemes, especially those sold on social media.

Step 1: an emergency fund

Life abroad comes with surprise costs: a broken boiler, a visa fee, a flight home for a family emergency. An emergency fund stops these turning into debt. Aim for three to six months of essential spending, saved in an easy-access account.

Step 2: understand ISAs

An Individual Savings Account (ISA) lets you save or invest without paying tax on the interest or growth. Each tax year there's an overall ISA allowance you can split between types:

  • Cash ISA: like a savings account, but the interest is tax-free
  • Stocks and Shares ISA: for investing in funds or shares; can rise and fall in value
  • Lifetime ISA: for eligible people saving for a first home or later life, with a government bonus but restrictions and penalties

You need to be UK resident to pay into an ISA. Check GOV.UK for the current allowance and rules, as they can change in Budgets.

Step 3: your workplace pension

If you're employed and eligible, you're automatically enrolled. You pay in, your employer pays in and you get tax relief. Staying in is usually one of the best returns you can get, because the employer contribution is effectively free money.

If you might leave the UK one day, your pension doesn't disappear. You can usually access it from abroad when you reach pension age, though transferring it overseas has complex rules and possible tax charges. Get regulated advice before doing that.

Step 4: investing for the long term

If you're investing, think long term (five years or more), spread your money across many companies with low-cost funds and don't put in money you'll need soon.

Red flags

  • Promises of guaranteed high returns
  • Pressure to invest quickly
  • "Forex trading" or crypto schemes promoted by friends or influencers
  • Companies not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority

Check the FCA register before handing over any money.

The bottom line

Build your safety net, use tax-free allowances, keep your pension and stay away from schemes that sound too good to be true.

This is general information, not financial advice.

posts.title: Owambe culture abroad: how Nigerian parties are thriving overseas
posts.excerpt: Aso ebi, jollof, live bands and money spraying. Nigerian parties have taken over event halls from London to Houston. Here's the culture and the etiquette.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Owambe, the big Nigerian party with matching outfits, live music, food and dancing, has become a fixture in diaspora communities abroad. Weddings, birthdays, naming ceremonies and anniversaries fill event halls in the UK, US and Canada. Here's what to expect and how to do it right, whether you're hosting or attending.

What makes an owambe

The word comes from Yoruba and roughly means "it is there", as in "the party is happening". Today it's used for any big, lively Nigerian celebration. Key ingredients include:

  • Aso ebi: matching fabric chosen by the celebrants, worn by family and friends
  • Food: jollof rice, fried rice, small chops, moin moin, pounded yam and soups
  • Music: a live band, DJ or both, often mixing highlife, juju, fuji and Afrobeats
  • Spraying money: guests dance and shower the celebrants with notes

How diaspora parties are different

Abroad, owambes adapt to new realities: hall bookings with strict finishing times, local noise rules, licensing for alcohol and higher costs. Many planners now run events with timetables to fit the venue's rules.

Etiquette for guests

  • RSVP honestly. Hall and catering costs are per head.
  • Buy the aso ebi if you can. It shows support. If you can't afford it, wear something in the colour theme.
  • Spray money respectfully. Many people now use smaller notes or pre-arranged bundles.
  • Bring a gift or give a card. Many couples share a gift list or bank details.

Tips for hosts

  • Book venues early. Popular halls fill up for summer weekends.
  • Check the venue's rules on music, alcohol, decorations and finishing times.
  • Have someone manage the programme so key moments don't run late.
  • Budget carefully; it's easy to overspend.

Bringing the next generation in

Owambes are a big way children raised abroad connect with Nigerian culture. They learn dances, dress up in traditional outfits and meet extended family and friends.

The bottom line

Owambe culture is alive and well abroad. Wear your aso ebi with pride, follow the venue rules and dance like nobody's watching.

posts.title: Studying in Canada: study permits, proof of funds and working while you study
posts.excerpt: Thinking of studying in Canada? Here's how study permits work, what proof of funds you'll need and the work rules for international students.
posts.content:
Quick gist: To study in Canada for more than six months, most international students need a study permit. You'll need an acceptance letter from a designated learning institution (DLI), proof that you can pay tuition and living costs and, for most applicants, a provincial attestation letter. Canada has been limiting the number of international student permits, so check the latest rules early.

Step 1: choose a designated learning institution

Only schools on IRCC's DLI list can enrol international students on a study permit. Check the list before applying, and research whether your programme makes you eligible for a post-graduation work permit if that matters to you.

Step 2: the provincial attestation letter

In recent years, Canada introduced a cap on study permits, and most applicants now need a provincial or territorial attestation letter (PAL or TAL) from the province where they'll study. Your school usually helps you get it. Some groups are exempt, so check IRCC guidance.

Step 3: proof of funds

You must show you can pay your first year's tuition plus living costs. The living cost amount was raised significantly in recent years and is updated over time, so check IRCC's current figure. Evidence can include bank statements, education loans, a Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC) or scholarship letters.

Make sure funds look genuine and consistent. Sudden large deposits without explanation can raise questions.

Step 4: apply

Apply online with your documents, pay the fees and give your biometrics. Processing times vary, so apply as early as possible.

Working while you study

Most full-time students with a valid study permit can work off campus up to a set number of hours per week during academic sessions and full-time during scheduled breaks. The weekly limit has changed in recent years, so check the current rule.

After you graduate

Some graduates can apply for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP). Eligibility now depends on factors like your programme and, for some, your field of study and language test results. Canadian work experience can help with permanent residence through Express Entry.

Watch out for

  • Agents who promise guaranteed visas
  • Fake admission letters
  • Programmes that don't lead to the work permit you're expecting

The bottom line

Canada remains a popular destination, but the rules are tighter than they were. Choose your school and programme carefully and plan your finances honestly.

This is general information, not immigration advice.

posts.title: Nigeria's 36 states and FCT: a quick guide for diaspora kids
posts.excerpt: Where is your family from? A simple guide to Nigeria's six geopolitical zones, 36 states and the FCT, perfect for children growing up abroad.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Nigeria is a federation of 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), where Abuja is located. The states are grouped informally into six geopolitical zones. Knowing the map helps children abroad understand where their family comes from and how diverse Nigeria is.

The basics

  • Capital: Abuja, in the FCT, which became the capital in 1991, replacing Lagos
  • Largest city: Lagos
  • States: 36, plus the FCT
  • Local government areas: 774

The six geopolitical zones

North Central: Benue, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Niger and Plateau, plus the FCT. Known for its farmland and the Jos Plateau.

North East: Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Taraba and Yobe. Home to Lake Chad's Nigerian shore and the Yankari Game Reserve.

North West: Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara. Kano is one of West Africa's oldest trading cities.

South East: Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu and Imo. Known for its traders, entrepreneurs and Igbo culture.

South South: Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Edo and Rivers. The Niger Delta region, centre of the oil industry, and home to Calabar's famous carnival.

South West: Ekiti, Lagos, Ogun, Ondo, Osun and Oyo. The Yoruba heartland and home to Lagos, Nigeria's commercial capital.

So many languages

Nigeria has more than 500 languages. The biggest groups are Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo, but there are many others, such as Ijaw, Kanuri, Ibibio, Tiv, Edo and Fulfulde. English is the official language, and Nigerian Pidgin is widely spoken.

Fun ways to teach children

  • Print a map and mark where each grandparent is from
  • Cook a dish from your state and another region
  • Watch Nollywood films set in different parts of Nigeria
  • Learn greetings in a few languages

The bottom line

Nigeria is big and beautifully diverse. Helping children understand the map is a simple, fun way to build their connection to home.

posts.title: Nigerian-heritage footballers and the 'which country' choice
posts.excerpt: Many top players born abroad have Nigerian parents. Here's how FIFA's eligibility rules work and why the choice between Nigeria and their birth country is so personal.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Many professional footballers born in the UK, Ireland, the US and elsewhere have Nigerian parents or grandparents, and some can choose to represent Nigeria or their country of birth. FIFA's rules allow a one-time switch of association in certain circumstances. The decision is often personal, balancing heritage, career and family.

A huge talent pool abroad

Nigerian communities in England, Ireland, Italy, Germany, the Netherlands and the US have produced many professional players. Some represent their country of birth, while others have chosen the Super Eagles. The Nigeria Football Federation regularly tries to persuade eligible players to commit.

How eligibility works

Under FIFA's rules, a player can be eligible for a country through birth, parents, grandparents or residence. Once a player has played competitive senior matches for one country, switching is usually not allowed, though FIFA allows a one-time change in limited cases, such as for players who played only a small number of matches before a certain age. The details are technical, which is why some switches take time to approve.

Why players choose Nigeria

  • Heritage and family pride
  • The chance to play at AFCON and World Cups
  • More playing time in a squad where they may start rather than sit on the bench
  • Connection to a passionate fanbase at home and in the diaspora

Why some choose their birth country

  • Where they grew up and feel most at home
  • Career ambitions with a team they believe has a better chance of winning major trophies
  • Commercial opportunities

Respect the decision

Fans sometimes take these decisions personally, but they're complicated choices for young people. Many players feel connected to both countries whatever they decide.

What it means for the Super Eagles

The ability to bring in diaspora-born talent gives Nigeria a deeper squad. Balancing these players with those developed at home is an ongoing conversation for coaches and fans.

The bottom line

Dual heritage is a strength. Whether a player chooses Nigeria or their birth country, the pride their families feel is the same.

posts.title: Working in the UK as a care worker: rights, pay and red flags
posts.excerpt: Thousands of Nigerians came to the UK as care workers. Here's what your rights are, how pay should work and the warning signs of exploitation.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Care workers in the UK have the same basic employment rights as other workers, including at least the National Minimum Wage, paid holiday and safe working conditions. Sponsored workers have extra protections. If an employer charges you for your sponsorship, takes your passport, doesn't give you the hours promised or threatens your visa, get advice quickly.

Your basic rights

  • Minimum wage: you must be paid at least the National Living Wage for every hour worked, including some travel time between visits for domiciliary carers.
  • Payslips: you have the right to an itemised payslip.
  • Holiday: most workers get 5.6 weeks of paid holiday a year (including bank holidays).
  • Breaks and rest: there are rules on rest breaks and maximum working hours.
  • Safe workplace: training and equipment to do the job safely.

Sponsored worker protections

If you're on a Health and Care Worker visa, your employer must pay you at least the salary stated on your Certificate of Sponsorship and meet their sponsor duties. They cannot make you pay for the Certificate of Sponsorship or the Immigration Skills Charge.

Red flags

  • Being charged large "recruitment" or "visa" fees
  • Your employer holding your passport or ID
  • Being given far fewer hours than promised
  • Pay below minimum wage or unpaid travel time
  • Threats about your visa if you complain
  • Being made to live in accommodation controlled by the employer at high cost

These can be signs of exploitation or modern slavery.

If your sponsor's licence is revoked

Some care providers have lost their sponsor licences. If that happens, you're usually given time to find a new sponsor or switch visa. Act quickly and get advice.

Where to get help

  • Acas: free advice on employment rights
  • Unseen helpline: for concerns about exploitation or modern slavery
  • Trade unions: many care workers join unions for support
  • Citizens Advice: general advice

You can also report sponsors who break the rules to the Home Office.

Protect yourself

Keep copies of your contract, CoS, payslips and rotas. Write down hours worked. Evidence makes it much easier to get help.

The bottom line

Care work is hard, valuable work, and you deserve fair treatment. Know your rights, keep records and get help early if something's wrong.

This is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Sending money to Nigeria: comparing banks, apps and agents
posts.excerpt: Banks, money transfer apps or the man at the African shop? Here's how to compare costs and safety when sending money to Nigeria.
posts.content:
Quick gist: The cheapest way to send money home is usually a regulated money transfer app or provider, but only if you compare the total cost: fee plus exchange-rate margin. Banks are often more expensive. Informal agents can look cheap but carry real risks. Always check that UK providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.

The real cost of sending money

Two things decide how much your family receives:

  1. The fee you pay to send
  2. The exchange rate the provider gives you, compared with the mid-market rate

A provider with zero fees but a poor rate can cost more than one with a small fee and a better rate. Compare how many naira arrive for the same amount of pounds.

Option 1: money transfer apps and providers

Specialist providers usually offer better rates than banks and fast payouts to Nigerian bank accounts. Under Nigeria's remittance rules, recipients usually receive naira, and international money transfer operators must be licensed by the CBN.

Check: FCA authorisation in the UK, transparent fees, good reviews and clear customer support.

Option 2: UK banks

Banks are convenient and secure but often charge higher fees and weaker exchange rates for international transfers. They can be useful for large, one-off transfers where you want extra paper trail, but compare first.

Option 3: informal agents

Some people use informal agents, often through community contacts, who promise a better rate. The risks:

  • No legal protection if money goes missing
  • Possible links to fraud or money laundering
  • Your bank account being frozen if it receives or sends suspicious funds

The small saving rarely justifies the risk.

Tips to save money

  • Send larger amounts less often if fees are fixed
  • Use promo rates for first transfers carefully; check what happens after
  • Set rate alerts in your app
  • Pay school fees and bills directly when possible

Stay safe

  • Double-check recipient account details
  • Beware of "urgent" requests from unknown numbers claiming to be relatives
  • Never send money to people you've only met online

The bottom line

Compare the total cost every time, stick to regulated providers and avoid shortcuts that could cost you everything.

This is general information, not financial advice.

posts.title: The Super Eagles' World Cup history: highs, lows and unforgettable moments
posts.excerpt: From USA 1994 to Russia 2018, Nigeria's World Cup journeys have given fans joy and heartbreak. Here's the story so far.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Nigeria first qualified for the FIFA World Cup in 1994 and has played in several tournaments since, reaching the round of 16 three times (1994, 1998 and 2014). The team has thrilled fans with its flair, but has also had painful exits and missed qualifications.

USA 1994: a dazzling debut

In their first World Cup, Nigeria topped a group that included Argentina and Bulgaria. In the round of 16 they led Italy until the final minutes, before Roberto Baggio's late goals sent Italy through. The world fell in love with the Super Eagles' attacking style.

France 1998: Spain stunned

Nigeria beat Spain 3–2 in one of the most memorable games of the tournament, with Sunday Oliseh's long-range strike becoming iconic. They topped their group again but lost to Denmark in the round of 16.

2002 and 2010: early exits

In Korea and Japan in 2002, and South Africa in 2010, Nigeria went out in the group stage, despite talented squads.

Brazil 2014: back to the knockouts

Under Stephen Keshi, fresh from winning AFCON 2013, Nigeria reached the round of 16 again, before losing to France.

Russia 2018: close but not enough

Nigeria beat Iceland but lost a tense final group game to Argentina, going out in the group stage.

Missing out

Nigeria missed the 2006 and 2022 World Cups, which hurt fans deeply. Each qualifying campaign is now watched closely by Nigerians at home and abroad.

The diaspora's World Cup

For Nigerians abroad, World Cup games are huge social events. Fans gather in homes, restaurants and community halls, often in full green-and-white, and many have travelled to tournaments to support the team.

The bottom line

Nigeria's World Cup story is full of brilliance and heartbreak. The dream of going further than the round of 16 lives on.

posts.title: Freelancing and remote work from abroad: what Nigerians need to know
posts.excerpt: Want to keep working for Nigerian clients or start a side hustle after moving? Your visa may not allow it. Here's what to check first.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Many people want to keep freelancing for Nigerian clients or start a side hustle after moving abroad. But your visa conditions decide what work you can do. Some visas restrict self-employment or extra work. Breaking the conditions can put your immigration status at risk, so check carefully before you start.

Why your visa matters

Every visa comes with conditions. In the UK, for example:

  • Skilled Worker and Health and Care Worker visas generally allow work for your sponsor, with limited additional work allowed in certain circumstances. Self-employment is usually not permitted.
  • Student visas usually limit working hours during term time and don't allow self-employment or freelancing.
  • Graduate visas usually allow most work, including self-employment.
  • Dependant visas often allow work, but check your specific conditions.
  • Indefinite Leave to Remain and citizenship generally remove these restrictions.

Rules differ in Canada, the US and other countries too.

Working for Nigerian clients while living in the UK

Some people assume that working remotely for a foreign client doesn't count. Immigration rules can still apply to work you do while physically in the UK, and tax rules apply too. Get advice before you take on remote work alongside a sponsored job or student visa.

Tax

If you're UK resident and earn self-employment income, you usually need to register with HMRC and file a Self Assessment tax return. Income earned abroad can also be taxable in the UK depending on your residence status.

Safer ways to build a side income

  • Wait until your visa allows self-employment
  • Focus on skills, certifications and networking in the meantime
  • Check if your visa allows permitted additional work in your sponsored field

The bottom line

Before you take on any side work, read your visa conditions and get advice if unsure. Protecting your status matters more than any extra income.

This is general information, not immigration or tax advice.

posts.title: Nigeria's Independence Day: how the diaspora celebrates 1 October
posts.excerpt: Every 1 October, Nigerians abroad wear green and white, cook jollof and celebrate. Here's the history and how diaspora communities mark the day.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Nigeria gained independence from British rule on 1 October 1960. Every year, Nigerians at home and abroad celebrate with parades, parties, church services, cultural shows and plenty of jollof. In diaspora cities, it's a day to show pride and pass culture on to children.

A short history

On 1 October 1960, Nigeria became an independent nation, with Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as prime minister. In 1963, Nigeria became a republic. The years since have brought civil war, military rule and the return to democracy in 1999, but Independence Day remains a symbol of national pride.

How the diaspora celebrates

  • Community events: associations host dinners, galas and cultural nights
  • Church and mosque services: prayers for Nigeria
  • Parades and festivals: some cities host Nigerian festivals and parades around the date
  • Schools: some children do presentations about Nigeria
  • Social media: a sea of green-and-white profile pictures and throwback photos

Ideas for families

  • Cook a traditional meal together
  • Watch a Nollywood classic or a documentary about Nigeria's history
  • Teach children the national anthem and pledge
  • Video call relatives back home
  • Wear traditional outfits to school or work events

Mixed feelings

For many people, the day is also a time to reflect on challenges at home. Celebrating while hoping for change is part of the diaspora experience.

The bottom line

Whatever you feel about the state of things, 1 October is a day to celebrate being Nigerian and to share that pride with the next generation.
